title: The Language of Animals
summary: Akbar wishes he could understand what animals say. Birbal shows him that understanding human suffering is far more urgent.
full_text:
While watching a flock of green parrots chirping in the palace mango trees, Emperor Akbar sighed wistfully: 'Birbal, how marvelous it would be if a king could understand the language of animals and birds! If I knew what the beasts were saying, I would be the wisest sovereign in history!'

Birbal smiled gently: 'Sire, the language of animals is simple: they speak of hunger, fear, affection, and weather. But understanding the silent language of human suffering is a far greater royal virtue.'

Akbar insisted: 'No, Birbal, find me a teacher who can teach me animal speech!'

Birbal promised to bring a master the following day.

The next morning, Birbal brought a poor, gaunt farmer into the Diwan-i-Khas. The farmer was trembling, holding a dry, withered stalk of wheat in his hands. He did not speak a word; he merely stood with downcast eyes, tears running silently down his hollow cheeks.

Akbar looked at the silent peasant in confusion: 'Birbal, who is this man? Why does he not speak? Is he the teacher of animal languages?'

Birbal answered with quiet gravity:

'Sire, this man speaks a language far more urgent than the chirping of birds. He speaks the silent language of drought, starvation, and despair.

'His dry wheat stalk tells you that the rains failed. His hollow cheeks tell you that his children have eaten only boiled wild roots for a month. His silent tears tell you that your tax collectors are threatening to seize his hut tomorrow morning.

'If an Emperor cannot understand the silent cries of his own suffering subjects, of what use is it to understand the chatter of monkeys and birds?'

Akbar was struck to the heart. He immediately ordered tax relief for the drought-stricken districts, distributed grain from the imperial granaries, and embraced Birbal for keeping his royal soul attuned to the cries of his people.
